contents.text: When the 1800s began, the United States was a young, growing nation. Most Americans lived in states along the Atlantic Coast. Most people lived and worked on farms, and most of their tools and other products were made by hand, often at home or by local craftspeople.

header.text: But in both Europe and the United States, changes had begun that would transform people's lives. Look at the timeline to learn about some of these changes. Then follow the instructions below.

alternativeText.text: A timeline of transformative changes in Europe and the United States. The changes in Europe are: in 1769, an improved steam engine is built in Scotland. In 1771, the first water-powered spinning mill to make yarn is built in England. In 1783, the world's first steam-powered ship is built in France. The changes in the United States are: in 1793, the first American spinning mill to make yarn is built in Rhode Island. In 1807, the first widely successful American steamboat is built in New York. In 1811, the U.S. government begins building its first national highway. In 1821, new mills in Massachussetts spin yarn and then weave it into fabric.

contents.text: In addition to water travel, land travel also improved in the early 1800s. At that time, many people from the Northeast were moving west to start farms, but travel was difficult. Once the settlers arrived, they also needed to send grain to customers back east, which took a long time.

. Begun in 1811, this highway ran west from Pennsylvania through Virginia, Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois. Because it took this route, the part of the country then called the Northwest became linked to the Northeast much more than to the South.

contents.text: Land transportation improved in the early 1800s, but it was still cheaper and faster for goods and people to be transported over water. Unfortunately, lakes and rivers often did not connect to make convenient shipping routes. So, goods had to be unloaded from a boat on one river, loaded onto horses or wagons, taken to the next river, and loaded onto boats again. Similar steps were necessary to avoid waterfalls and rapids.

pieces.text: To make shipping more efficient, states began to dig long, shallow canals to connect lakes and rivers. The most successful was the
, constructed between 1817 and 1825. The Erie Canal connected Lake Erie to the Hudson River, which then connected to New York City.

content.text: The route of the Erie Canal

contents.text: The Erie Canal had significant effects, in New York and beyond. Match each fact about the Erie Canal to its effect.

draggableItems.text: People around the Great Lakes could more easily buy clothes made on the East Coast.
Other states spent millions of dollars to build their own canals, hoping to make a profit as large as New York's.
New York City became the nation's busiest port and its leading business center.

staticItems.text: The state of New York spent $7,000,000 on the canal. But the state earned even more money by charging people to use the canal.
Goods such as wheat could be shipped from areas near the Great Lakes, across the Erie Canal, and then down the Hudson River to New York City.
The cost of shipping products from east to west decreased sharply, so those products became cheaper for many westerners.

questions.text: Candidates for office could use newspapers to reach more voters than ever before, even in remote areas.

contents.text: Land transportation improved in the early 1800s, but it was still cheaper and faster for goods and people to be transported over water. Unfortunately, lakes and rivers often did not connect to make convenient shipping routes. So, goods had to be unloaded from a boat on one river, loaded onto horses or wagons, taken to the next river, and loaded onto boats again. Similar steps were necessary to avoid waterfalls and rapids.

pieces.text: To make shipping more efficient, states began to dig long, shallow canals to connect lakes and rivers. The most successful was the
, constructed between 1817 and 1825. The Erie Canal connected Lake Erie to the Hudson River, which then connected to New York City.

content.text: The route of the Erie Canal

contents.text: The Erie Canal had significant effects, in New York and beyond. Match each fact about the Erie Canal to its effect.

draggableItems.text: The cost of shipping products from east to west decreased sharply, so those products became cheaper.
Goods such as wheat could be shipped from areas near the Great Lakes, across the Erie Canal, and then down the Hudson River to New York City.
The state of New York spent $7,000,000 on the canal. But it earned even more money by charging people to use the canal.

staticItems.text: People around the Great Lakes could more easily buy clothes made on the East Coast.
Other states spent millions of dollars to build their own canals, hoping to make a profit as large as New York's.
New York City became the nation's busiest port and its leading business center.

contents.text: When the 1800s began, the United States was a young, growing nation. Most Americans lived in states along the Atlantic Coast. Most people lived and worked on farms, and most of their tools and other products were made by hand, often at home or by local craftspeople.

header.text: But in both Europe and the United States, changes had begun that would transform people's lives. Look at the timeline to learn about some of these changes. Then follow the instructions below.

alternativeText.text: A timeline of transformative changes in Europe and the United States. The changes in Europe are: in 1769, an improved steam engine is built in Scotland. In 1771, the first water-powered spinning mill to make yarn is built in England. In 1783, the world's first steam-powered ship is built in France. The changes in the United States are: in 1793, the first American spinning mill to make yarn is built in Rhode Island. In 1807, the first widely successful American steamboat is built in New York. In 1811, the U.S. government begins building its first national highway. In 1821, new mills in Massachussetts spin yarn and then weave it into fabric.

contents.text: Land transportation improved in the early 1800s, but it was still cheaper and faster for goods and people to be transported over water. Unfortunately, lakes and rivers often did not connect to make convenient shipping routes. So, goods had to be unloaded from a boat on one river, loaded onto horses or wagons, taken to the next river, and loaded onto boats again. Similar steps were necessary to avoid waterfalls and rapids.

contents.text: When the 1800s began, the United States was a young, growing nation. Most Americans lived in states along the Atlantic Coast. Most people lived and worked on farms, and most of their tools and other products were made by hand, often at home or by local craftspeople.

header.text: But in both Europe and the United States, changes had begun that would transform people's lives. Look at the timeline to learn about some of these changes. Then answer the question below.

alternativeText.text: A timeline of transformative changes in Europe and the United States. The changes in Europe are: in 1769, an improved steam engine is built in Scotland. In 1771, the first water-powered spinning mill to make yarn is built in England. In 1783, the world's first steam-powered ship is built in France. The changes in the United States are: in 1793, the first American spinning mill to make yarn is built in Rhode Island. In 1807, the first widely successful American steamboat is built in New York. In 1811, the U.S. government begins building its first national highway. In 1821, new mills in Massachussetts spin yarn and then weave it into fabric.

subpoints.text: The ship was designed to hold 454 enslaved people, but it was often overloaded, carrying as many as 740 people. subheader.text: What was the journey like?

subpoints.text: The ship was designed to hold 454 enslaved people, but it was often overloaded, carrying as many as 740 people. To fit that many people, captains and sailors made enslaved people lie on their sides instead of their backs. Enslaved people were chained in place for most of the journey. They were brought up to the main deck for meals, but they spent most of their days lying in darkness.

contents.text: Did you know that the state of Texas was once an independent country? In the following questions, you will learn about Texas independence and how Texas became part of the United States.

The following timeline shows some important events in Texas history and United States history in the 1700s and 1800s. Events in Texas history are below the timeline. Events in U.S. history are above the timeline. Look at the timeline. Then follow the instructions below.

alternativeText.text: A timeline spanning from 1700 to 1850. In 1718, Spain built forts across Texas to claim the area. In 1776, the United States declared its independence from Great Britain. In 1821, Mexico, whose territory included Texas, won its independence from Spain. In 1836, Texas gained independence from Mexico and became its own country. In 1845, Texas joined the United States as the 28th state.

Mexico refused to agree to the independence of Texas. Meanwhile, the independent Texas government asked the United States to annex it. Even though Mexico warned the United States that annexation would be considered an act of war, the United States annexed Texas anyway.

subpoints.text: According to the Supreme Court, banning slavery took away slaveholders' constitutional right to own property. In this case, the property was enslaved people. Under this ruling, slavery could spread to every territory.

case outraged many Americans, especially in the North. They thought that slaveholders were gaining too much power. In 1858, an Illinois Republican named
gave a speech about the role of slavery in the United States. Match each part of the adapted text from the speech with its meaning.

draggableItems.text: The United States cannot survive forever if the country is divided over slavery.
…or those in favor of slavery will ensure that it is spread to the entire country.
Perhaps people will stop new slave states from being created and eventually put an end to slavery…
Do you think I'm wrong? Take a look at what the Supreme Court just did.

staticItems.text: A house divided against itself cannot stand. I believe this government cannot endure permanently, half slave, and half free.
I do not expect the Union to be dissolved…but I do expect it will cease to be divided – It will become all one thing, or all the other.

…or its supporters will push it forward till it shall become alike lawful in all the states, old, as well as new.

In his House Divided speech, Abraham Lincoln used the metaphor of a house divided to describe

. Lincoln meant that the political divisions in the United States made it similar to an unstable house. He stated that having the country split between free and slave states could not last forever. Lincoln argued that it caused too many political divisions, and that sooner or later the country would have to make a final decision about slavery.

contents.text: In order to manufacture clothing, the United Kingdom imported a large amount of cotton. Before the Civil War, the United Kingdom imported most of its cotton from the Southern states.

The graph below shows cotton imports for the United Kingdom. The graph's data starts with 1860, the year that Southern states began to secede, and ends with 1864, the last full year of the Civil War. Look at the graph. Then follow the instructions below.

alternativeText.text: A line graph titled "Cotton imports into the United Kingdom, 1860-1864." In 1860, the United Kingdom imported about 400,000 tons of cotton. Almost all of this cotton came from the United States. From 1861-1864, this changed significantly: Imports from the United States fell below 300,000 tons in 1861, below 75,000 tons in 1862, then below 50,000 tons in 1863 and 1864. Meanwhile, imports from other countries were steadily increasing. The United Kingdom imported less than 25,000 tons of cotton from Egypt in 1860, but over 50,000 tons in 1864. The United Kingdom also imported less than 25,000 tons of cotton from India in 1860, which sharply increased to around 130,000 tons in 1861 and continued increasing to over 200,000 tons in 1864.

subpoints.text: Cotton played an important part in the global economy of the 1800s. Plantation owners sent raw cotton to mills in places such as New England and the United Kingdom. These mills would then turn the cotton into clothing and bedding. From shippers to merchants to mill workers, hundreds of thousands of people outside the South depended on cotton to earn their livelihoods.

alternativeText.text: A line graph titled "Cotton imports into the United Kingdom, 1860-1864." In 1860, the United Kingdom imported about 400,000 tons of cotton. subheader.text: Why did Hammond believe cotton made the South powerful?

subpoints.text: Cotton played an important part in the global economy of the 1800s. Plantation owners sent raw cotton to mills in places such as New England and the United Kingdom. A map that shows territory gained by the Union between 1861 and 1865. In 1861, the Union retook territory in Missouri, northern Kentucky, northern West Virginia, Delaware, and Maryland.

text.text: Most early battles of the Civil War are fought in Southern states. The Confederate Army wins many of these battles.

The Civil War ends. The Union defeats the Confederacy, keeping the United States together. The U.S. government bans slavery.
